E. P. Roe's Taken Alive, volume eleven of his works, gathers stories with an autobiography, under the heading A Native Author Called Roe. Its contents include Taken Alive itself, in chapters on something before unknown. A visitor at the mine, thwarted hopes, and what Brandt saw follow. Christmas Eve follows, with Found Yet Lost, Love in the Wilderness, and Love at Home after it.

Roe writes moral, domestic stories of American life, with illustrations in the original. The volume offers readers both fiction and the author's own account of his career. It shows why Roe was one of the most popular American novelists of his day.
5734-life-in-the-grey-nunnery-at-montrea:
Sarah Richardson presents Life in the Grey Nunnery at Montreal as an authentic narrative of convent life. Chapters move from parentage and a father's marriage through the white nunnery, the nursery, a slave for life, confirmation, the grey nunnery, an orphan's home, and confession and sorrow of no avail. Later chapters promise alone with the dead, the sick nun, and at last the joy of freedom.

Readers should treat the book as a period exposé narrative, a popular genre that claimed inside knowledge of closed institutions. Its power comes from personal testimony, whether readers accept its claims or read it as polemic. Historians of religion, gender, and anti-Catholic literature will find it a vivid example of nineteenth-century convent tales and the fears they fed.
6116-out-of-the-primitive:
Robert Ames Bennet opens Out of the Primitive with castaways north of the Zambezi, where a little tramp rescue steamer runs miles into the offing and lays to through dark hours. Coral reefs fringing Africa's southeast coast make moonless nights decidedly undesirable for such a vessel.

The Earl of Avondale steps from a close, hot stateroom into coolness before dawn, reads the Southern Cross to port, and knows the steamer heads for the coast. Phosphorescent light crinkles the black sea under a faint breeze heavy with rotting vegetation. Bennet sets a tale of rank, wreck, and wilderness survival.
6373-the-luck-of-roaring-camp-and-other-:
Bret Harte's volume gathers the Luck of Roaring Camp and other tales with condensed novels, Spanish and American legends, and earlier papers, introduced by the author. In 1882 his scattered work was brought into five compact volumes, and in 1897 his publishers undertook a uniform presentation of more than thirty years of poems, tales, sketches, and romances. This book samples that long output in one place.

A bright October day in the California Sierras opens one tale, with a sylvan lake, an Indian village's smoke among lofty pines, and Judge Tompkins's log cottage among buckeyes. Inside, goldfish in an aquarium and a grand piano show cultivation within a humble exterior, while paintings from Van Dyke to Turner hang on the walls. Harte writes the west with irony and tenderness, where rough camps hold refined hearts.
6616-december-love:
Robert Hichens opens in a London club, where Francis Braybrooke, a man who knows everybody, sits down beside Alick Craven of the Foreign Office. Braybrooke loves people, not ideas, and cannot live away from the center of human doings; new faces are his delight. Craven, back from war service, listens as talk turns to love late in life.

December Love, as its title hints, weighs passion that comes when youth has passed, with all its grace and risk. Hichens writes with a social novelist's eye for talk, manners, and the small shifts of feeling. The novel is a polished, adult romance of London life, where age does not end desire.
6670-christmas-eve:
Robert Browning's Christmas Eve bursts out of a little chapel into fresh night air, after rain drove in gusts down the common. The speaker waited five minutes in the doorway, then squeezed past fumbling hands at the inner door, into a sheepfold entry six feet long by three feet wide. He blocked half of it, eyed like a wild beast by the flock within.

From that cramped, comic start, the poem moves into a wide vision of faith, doubt, and Christmas night. Browning's verse is dense, vivid, and full of sudden turns. Christmas Eve is a great, strange poem, where a rainy chapel visit opens onto questions of belief itself.
740-remarks-of-mr-calhoun-of-south-carol:
John C. Calhoun spoke in the Senate on 15 February 1833 on nullification and the Force Bill, at the height of the clash over tariffs. South Carolina had claimed the right to void federal law, and Congress debated a bill to enforce it by force. Calhoun rose to defend his state and to press the limits of federal power.

His speech opens on the public debt, declared all but paid, and on the hopes that died with a long, fruitless session. From there he argues the case for state rights against coercion. The text is a key source for the nullification crisis, showing Calhoun's logic at its sharpest and the temper of a Union under strain.
7890-blind-love:
Wilkie Collins's Blind Love, completed by Walter Besant, runs through three periods of mounting intrigue. The first brings sour French wine, a man refused, a registered packet, and Mountjoy's game, lost, replayed, and won, beside a doctor doctored and a father's message.

Later Iris moves between home, Hampstead Heath, London, and Paris, through a lady's maid, a keyhole, a hospital mystery, and a school for husbands. Lord Harry's honeymoon, a decree of fate, and my lord's and my lady's minds close a tale of love, drink, and deceit, finished after Collins's death.
7891-the-dead-alive:
Wilkie Collins's The Dead Alive opens in a barrister's chambers in the Temple. A doctor tells Philip Lefrank his heart and lungs are sound: his disease is overwork, his remedy rest. Lefrank, a junior barrister from Jersey, faints at his desk and fears ruin if he stops, with briefs piled high in term time.

The tale that follows turns on a sick man, a supposed death, and a mystery of identity. Collins tells it with a knack for legal detail and surprise. Through courts, illness, and a life hung in doubt, the short novel asks who is truly dead, and what proof can bring a lost man back.
7971-the-fugitive:
Rabindranath Tagore's The Fugitive, dedicated to W. W. Pearson, gathers dramatic poems and translations in three parts. The first pairs Kacha and Devayani, the second Ama and Vinayaka with a mother's prayer, and the third Somaka and Ritvik with Karna and Kunti. The opening lines address an eternal fugitive whose rushing steps sweep the dust of the world into sweetness and shake a sacred shower of death over life.

The pieces draw on Indian legend and myth, retold in Tagore's lyrical English. They are best read aloud or slowly, for their music and imagery carry much of their meaning. For readers coming to Tagore through his poems, this volume shows his dramatic imagination at work, and his habit of finding spiritual questions inside old stories.
8073-a-fool-for-love:
Francis Lynde, author of The Grafters and The Master of Appleby, wrote this railroad romance opening on a December morning in Kansas City. The Chicago and Alton's fast train, dripping from a rush through the wet night, steams into Union Station, and the chapters that follow move through switched engines. Changed itineraries, crystalline altitudes, a landslide, a rajah's order, the majesty of the law, block signals, spiked switches, and the right of way.

The novel mixes adventure with love, using the railroad as both setting and plot engine: schedules, signals, and wrecks decide fates. Lynde knew railroad life well, and his technical detail gives the romance ballast. For readers who enjoy early twentieth-century adventure fiction, it is a fast, vivid ride.
8076-the-history-of-david-grieve:
Mrs Humphry Ward, author of Robert Elsmere, told the history of David Grieve in four books: childhood, youth, storm and stress, and maturity. The novel opens in dialect, with David and his sister Louie on the steps of a house, a battered hat, and a tall, bony woman insisting the hat be tied on. From that northern childhood, David grows through work, love, and religious doubt toward a hard-won adult life.

Ward writes a Victorian novel of formation, attentive to class, industry, and faith in a changing England. David's story is long and serious, in the tradition of the bildungsroman, and it was widely read in its day. For readers of George Eliot and Thomas Hardy, it offers a comparable, if less famous, study of a young life shaped by place and conscience.
8664-the-glory-of-the-conquered-the-stor:
Susan Glaspell published this 1909 novel, dedicated to Dr A. L. Hageboeck, who made the book possible, as the story of a great love tested by illness and ambition. Part one follows Ernestine, a painter, and Karl, a scientist, through letters, homecomings, studio and laboratory, and a verdict that darkens their future. Science, art, and love are set against one another, and a warning and a premonition hang over the closing chapters.

Part two carries the couple into the consequences, where love must survive not triumph but loss and change. Glaspell, later a Pulitzer-winning playwright, writes with psychological care about a woman artist and a man of science. The glory of the conquered, the title suggests, lies in enduring rather than winning. Readers will find a serious early feminist novel, more interested in inner life than in plot fireworks.
9247-fragments-from-the-journal-of-a-sol:
Hawthorne's fragments from a solitary man's journal open with his poor friend Oberon, now asleep with the silent ages. Oberon died calmly of lung disease, his life ebbing like a tide, not flickering like a wasted lamp. His last words asked his friend to burn his papers, fearing some might be betrayed into print.

The old disconnected journal in the narrator's hands survived that plea, and these fragments come from it. They read as notes of a lonely mind, musing on life, death, and art. The piece remains a haunting scrap from Hawthorne's workshop, intimate and unfinished by design.
93-tom-sawyer-detective:
Tom Sawyer turns detective when a diamond robbery ends in murder on his uncle's farm. Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer, Detective sends Tom and Huck to Arkansas, where Uncle Silas stands accused. Twain notes the plot comes from a real Swedish criminal trial.

Three sleepers, a ghostly talk, and the finding of Jupiter Dunlap build the case. Tom spots the flaw in the prosecution and names the true killers. The accused confesses in public, as in the source trial. The short novel mixes frontier humor with a fair-play mystery. The mystery's fairness, with clues laid plain, pleased readers who love to solve alongside Tom.
9603-hung-lou-meng-or-the-dream-of-the-r:
Book one of Hung Lou Meng, or The Dream of the Red Chamber, opens Cao Xueqin's great Chinese novel in H. Bencraft Joly's translation. Joly, a British consular man in China, began the work as a student in Peking, puzzled by the novel's maze. His preface, dated Macao, September 1891, owns faults in prose and rhyme, but hopes to aid students of Chinese. The tale opens with Chen Shih-yin in a vision.

Chia Yü-ts'un enters a dusty world of fate, dreams, and great houses, as the Jia family's fortunes unfold. Verse, dreams, and household intrigue mix from the first chapter. A reader gets the gateway to one of the world's great novels, in a pioneer's English version.
9604-hung-lou-meng-or-the-dream-of-the-r:
Book two of Hung Lou Meng, or The Dream of the Red Chamber, continues Cao Xueqin's great Chinese novel, here in H. Bencraft Joly's translation. Chapter twenty-five opens with dark arts at work on Pao-yü and Lady Feng, who meet five devils. The gem of spiritual perception, in a fit of torpor, meets two perfect men. Hsiao Hung's troubled dream of Chia Yün sets the chapter's eerie tone.

Later scenes follow the great Jia household through love, spite, and fate, as dreams blur with waking life. Joly's version brings Qing dynasty manners, verse, and intrigue to English readers. A reader gets a further stretch of one of the world's great novels, rich in family drama and Buddhist-Taoist wonder.
a-bit-o-love:
John Galsworthy sets his play in a village of the West of England, with the action passing on Ascension Day, as the scene list states. The persons include Michael Strangway, a curate with strange, tender ideas, his wife Beatrice, and the farmers and laborers of the parish: Burlacombes, Trustafords, Jarlands, and Freemans. Strangway's charity toward a thief has set the village against him.

Three acts move between Strangway's rooms, the village inn, the churchyard, and a barn. His wife has left him for another man, and the parish wants a harder, more respectable priest. Galsworthy writes the West Country speech with care and treats both the curate's gentleness and the villagers' rough justice with sympathy.
a-daughter-of-eve:
Honoré de Balzac builds his novel around two sisters, the Maries of his first chapter's title, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. One sister has married for rank and lives in Parisian society; the other has married a banker and keeps a respectable home. A confidence between the sisters opens the tale, and a celebrated man enters it.

Chapters follow the actress Florine, a romantic love pursued through letters, rising debt, and a crisis named plainly in the contents: Suicide. The husband's triumph closes the book. Balzac studies how boredom, vanity, and fine feeling can wreck a good woman in a world that watches women closely and judges them harshly.
a-dozen-ways-of-love: Lily Dougall explores a dozen ways of love in short stories. Her chapters treat young love, a marriage made in heaven, thrift, a taint in the blood, and witchcraft. Other tales follow a commercial traveler, a syndicate baby, and a girl who believed in love. Dougall writes of love in its many forms with sympathy and wit.
a-fool-for-love: Francis Lynde tells of a fool for love aboard a limited train. The hero takes passage in a Missouri December, and an engine switched and an itinerary changed set the plot moving. Chapters follow a landslide, a rajah's order, and the majesty of the law. Lynde writes a railroad romance of adventure and devotion.
a-zola-dictionary-the-characters-of-the-:
J. G. Patterson's A Zola Dictionary, prepared at Edinburgh in May 1912, indexes the people of Émile Zola's Rougon-Macquart novels. A biographical and critical introduction opens the volume. Synopses of the plots follow, arranged in the reading order Zola himself indicated. A map and the family's genealogical tree complete the apparatus.

Twenty novels and hundreds of characters pass under Patterson's alphabetical hand. Each entry condenses a life from Zola's own words, so far as condensation allowed. He relied on the recognized biographies by Alexis, Sherrard, and Vizetelly, his prefatory note records. The dictionary serves readers lost in the vast clan of Rougons and Macquarts, legitimate and illegitimate branches alike. Heredity, Zola's ruling idea, becomes visible in the tree. Reference works date quickly, but this one preserves how Edwardian England organized its Zola.
adventures-of-a-sixpence-in-guernsey-by-: A Native of Guernsey follows a single sixpence as it passes from hand to hand around the island, letting each new owner tell a piece of local life. Through shopkeepers, sailors, and country folk, the coin's journey sketches Guernsey manners, trades, and talk in the mid-nineteenth century. The device gives the book both a light plot and a portrait of an island community.
affairs-of-state-being-an-account-of-cer: Burton Egbert Stevenson sends an American family into comic peril in the land of windmills, where court intrigue and romance upset their holiday plans. The story follows wiles, disguises, and narrow escapes as ordinary travellers are swept into affairs of state far above their station. Light, brisk, and good-humoured, it is an early example of the Ruritanian romance.
american-political-ideas-viewed-from-the: John Fiske delivers American political ideas viewed from universal history, in lectures given at the Royal Institution of Great Britain in May 1880. Dedicated in spirit to Tocqueville, the lectures place American democracy in a long story of political growth. Fiske argues with clarity and optimism for the federal idea as a stage in human progress.
angel-agnes-the-heroine-of-the-yellow-fe: Charles Wesley Alexander tells of Angel Agnes, the heroine of the yellow fever plague in Shreveport. The story honours a woman whose nursing and courage stood out when fever struck the city. Alexander's account preserves a local heroine's memory, in the sentimental style of its time. Her name lived on in local praise long after.
bibb-narrative:
Henry Bibb published his Narrative of his life and adventures in 1849. Born enslaved in Kentucky, Bibb escaped more than once, and each recapture cost him dearly. The book became a bestseller in the abolitionist movement.

Bibb tells how he left his wife and child to gain freedom, then risked return trips to free them. He describes slave markets, patrols, and the grief of families torn apart. His path later crossed the Cherokee country, where slavery also held Native people. Bibb went on to edit a Black newspaper in Canada for refugee readers. His account includes letters and notices meant to prove his tale true.
brown-narrative:
William Wells Brown escaped slavery in Missouri in 1834 and published his Narrative in 1847. Brown had worked as a steamboat hand on the Mississippi, which gave him his chance to run. The book went through several editions in a few years.

He tells of his hire to a slave trader, the coffles on the road, and the suffering he witnessed. After escape he became an abolitionist lecturer in America and Britain. Brown later wrote Clotel, often called the first novel by an African American. His Narrative shows the keen storyteller he already was on the lecture stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Sainte-Geneviève describes the Paris abbey founded by King Clovis as a college of clerics, later canons regular. By 1147 secular canons officiated there, but Louis the Seventh and the pope, witnessing disorders, resolved to restore regular discipline.

At Suger and St. Bernard's request, Gildwin, first Abbot of Saint-Victor, sent Odo, his prior, to lead the reform. Difficulties followed, but order prevailed and some canons joined, including the young Canon William, famed for virtue and learning. At Bishop Absalon of Roskild's request William went to Denmark to reform a monastery on the Isle of Eskil, enduring trials, obstacles and persecutions in the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltasar-de-e:
Baltasar de Echave, called the Elder, was a painter born at Zumaya in Spain late in the sixteenth century. He died in Mexico about the middle of the seventeenth century. He ranked among the earliest Spanish artists to reach Mexico, arriving with Sebastian Arteaga and Alonzo Vasquez. Tradition says his wife, also a painter, taught him.

His subjects were chiefly religious, and his skill in composition, charm of color, and tenderness recall Guercino. The National Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City holds many of his best pictures, from the Adoration of the Magi to Saint Cecilia. More hang in the Profesa church, and fifteen altar panels stand in Santiago Tlaltelolco. His cathedral Candelaria and a San Sebastian are also noted, the latter believed to be his wife's work. He also wrote on the Biscayan language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-kervyn-:
Baron Kervyn de Lettenhove was a Belgian statesman and writer of history, born near Bruges in 1817, who died there in 1891. Sent to the Chamber of Representatives in 1861, he debated foreign affairs and public schools keenly. In 1870 his party took power, and he received the Interior post. A mistaken Limburg governor pick forced him to quit, and he slowly left politics for history work.

Already in 1856 the French Academy had crowned his Studies on Froissart's Chronicles. Touring Europe's book rooms and archives, he gathered data that revised common views on several points. His grave, polished, somewhat puffed-up style drew charges of bias to Elizabeth, William the Silent, and Marnix, without sufficient reason. His major works span Flanders's history, Commines's letters, Burgundian Belgium, Mary Stuart, and ties with England under Philip II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-categorical-i:
The categorical imperative is Immanuel Kant's term for the moral law as reason itself lays it down. Kant starts from the good will. Only a will that acts from duty, out of respect for the law and not from inclination or hoped-for results, counts as good without qualification. The law commands respect because it is universal and necessary, binding every rational being alike.

Kant states the rule as acting only on a maxim that could hold as a universal law for all rational beings. The article then weighs this account against Kant's own theoretical philosophy, noting a tension between the two that makes moral necessity look close to fatalism. Kant set out the imperative in 1785 and again in his Critique of Practical Reason in 1788.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citta-della-p:
Citta della Pieve, a city of obscure origin in Umbria's Perugia province, was certainly an episcopal see by the eleventh century. In 1099 its bishop was expelled by the Ghibellines. Paschal the Second later joined it to the Diocese of Chiusi. Clement the Eighth re-established it as a separate see in 1601, with Fabrizio Paolucci of the Counts of Cabulo as first bishop.

In 1642, while Giovanni Battista Carcarasio was bishop, German soldiers of the Duke of Parma sacked the city. The diocese answers directly to the Holy See. Its cathedral, dedicated to Saints Gervasius and Protasius, was reportedly built at Saint Ambrose's urging. The diocese counts sixty thousand people, thirty-three parishes, eighty-six churches and chapels, sixty-five secular priests, and four houses of women religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conclave:
Austin Dowling's entry explains the conclave, from Latin cum, with, and clavis, key: a place securely closed. It means both the closed hall prepared for cardinals electing a pope and the assembly itself. In present form it dates from the end of the thirteenth century. Earlier ways of filling Peter's See belong to the Papal Elections entry. Dowling treats the method's history and the ceremonial itself.

History opens at Viterbo in 1271, where an election dragged over two years and nine months until local authorities shut the cardinals in. Stringent rules drew opposition, yet early conclave elections proved the principle sound. Ceremonial runs from the camerlengo's verification of the pope's death to the walling off of Vatican apartments, cells for cardinals and conclavists, perhaps two hundred and fifty persons inside. Four forms of election stand: scrutinium, compromissum, accessus, and quasi-inspiratio, with secret ballot and a two-thirds vote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dove:
The dove appears in Christian antiquity both as a symbol and as a vessel for the Eucharist. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry finds it most often as a sign of the Holy Spirit, above all in scenes of the baptism of Christ and of Pentecost. Saint Gregory the Great is shown with a dove on his shoulder, marking inspiration and divine guidance. After Clovis's baptism, a dove of gold was hung in the baptistery at Reims.

Dove-shaped vessels were also hung over baptismal fonts, and the dove marked martyrdom, showing the Spirit granting fortitude. Gifts of silver towers with golden doves from Constantine and later popes fill the old papal book of lives. The entry thus follows one gentle bird through art, liturgy, and the treasures of Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eve:
Eve is the first woman of the Bible, wife of Adam and mother of Cain, Abel, and Seth. Her Hebrew name, Hawwah, appears only five times in Scripture, and Genesis links it with the verb to live, since she was mother of all the living. The Bible's account of her lies almost wholly in Genesis chapters two, three, and four. The first story tells simply that mankind was made male and female, while the second tells how God formed woman from man's rib.

In the story of the Fall, the serpent tempts Eve, she tempts Adam, and shame and remorse follow their eating. For her share she is sentenced to sorrow in childbirth and to life under her husband's power. Yet God also promises enmity between her seed and the serpent, until her seed, the future Redeemer, crushes its head.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-expectative:
Expectative means the advance grant of a church benefice that is not yet vacant. It falls vacant in due course, regularly on the death of its present holder. The Third Lateran Council in 1179 forbade such promises, renewing an older ban, and Boniface VIII widened the ban. Yet through the Middle Ages chapters still gave expectatives for canon stalls, and the Holy See let chapters name four canons that way.

Popes from the twelfth century granted them straight, and charged another churchman with investing the appointee later. Delegates of the Holy See, universities, and certain princes also won the privilege, with limits. The practice bred grave abuses, above all during the Western Schism. Trent swept expectatives away, save a coadjutor named with right of succession for bishops and abbots, plus prefects Apostolic. Trent allows the only expectatives still in use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-jean-ba:
Felix Neve was a Belgian Orientalist and philologist of the University of Louvain. Born at Ath in 1816, he took his doctorate at Louvain in 1838. He studied under Lassen, Tiersch, and Burnouf at Bonn, Munich, and Paris. In 1841 he took the university chair of Greek and Latin literature.

Neve taught Sanskrit at Louvain for thirty-six years with unsparing energy and success. He translated chosen Rig-Veda hymns and the Indian drama of Rama's story. He also worked on Armenian texts, prayers, hymns, and histories. Retired in 1877, he published steadily for fifteen more years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-perreyv:
Paris priest Henri Perreyve, born in 1831 to a law professor, gave up law for philosophy and theology and helped restore the Oratory in France. With the Perraud brothers and Father Gratry under Father Pététol, he rebuilt the congregation and was ordained in 1858. He served as chaplain at Lycée Saint-Louis and took the Sorbonne chair of church history in 1861 until illness stopped his lectures.

Friend to Ozanam, Montalembert, Cochin, and Lacordaire, he won young men above all by a kind and affectionate nature. His works include a critique of the Gospels of 1859, talks on the Catholic Church, a sick person's day, biographies and panegyrics, and first communion memories. Sermons and meditations on John and on holy orders complete the list. Letters were published after his early death in 1865.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-cosgrov:
Henry Cosgrove, second Bishop of Davenport, Iowa, was born at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1834 and emigrated to Iowa with his parents in 1845. Ordained priest in 1857, he took charge of St. Marguerite's Church, Davenport, in 1861, and after Bishop McMullen's death administered the diocese before his own consecration on 20 July 1884. He was the first native-born American named to a see west of the Mississippi.

Short as this entry is, it marks a turning point in the American hierarchy: leadership passing from missionary bishops sent from abroad to men raised on the frontier they would govern. Cosgrove died at Davenport on 23 December 1906, having spent nearly half a century in the service of the Iowa church he had joined as an eleven-year-old immigrant child.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-capgrave:
John Capgrave was an Augustinian friar, historian, and theologian of fifteenth-century Norfolk. Born at Lynn in 1393, he was ordained about 1417 and professed an Augustinian at Lynn. He became doctor of divinity and later provincial of his order, and died at Lynn in 1464.

His name is best known for the Nova Legenda Angliae, the first full collection of English saints' lives. It was really compiled by John of Tynemouth and only edited and rearranged by Capgrave. Apart from that, his own works prove unusual scholarship: lives of Henry VI's worthies, of Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, and of St. Gilbert and St. Katharine, a Chronicle of England to 1417, commentaries on many Bible books, a work on the creeds, and sermons and lectures, many still in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josse-clichto:
Josse Clichtove was a Flemish theologian of the Sorbonne who fought Luther with pen and council. Born at Nieuport in 1472, he studied at Louvain and Paris, took his theology doctorate in 1506, and became a Sorbonne professor. In 1515 he took charge of the studies of Louis Guillard, bishop-elect of Tournai, and followed him to Tournai and Chartres.

Clichtove began with commentaries on Aristotle and the Fathers and early championed reform of studies. Later he gave himself almost wholly to opposing Luther, gathering the Council of Sens' arguments into a volume and writing Antilutherus and a defense of the Church against Lutheran claims. His works span nearly every branch of theology and philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-love:
Love, in theology called charity, is the third and greatest of the divine virtues named by Paul. It is a gift poured into the heart that moves the will to cherish God above all things, and people for God's sake. It differs from natural liking, since it comes by divine infusion with sanctifying grace.

Its seat lies in the rational will, not in feeling alone. Its act is benevolent friendship: wishing God all honour and seeking it for him, as friends seek good for friends. Its motive is God's own goodness, loved for itself, not for reward, and its range covers God and neighbour alike. Later sections weigh hope, self-love, and the order of loving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nave:
A nave, architecturally, is the central, open space of a church, west of the choir or chancel, separated from it by a low wall or screen. Columns, shafts or piers divide it from the side aisles. It is roofed with timber or vaulted in masonry, and usually rises above the aisle roofs for high windows. Colloquially the term covers the worshippers' portion, including central and side aisles and crossing transepts.

The name comes from Latin navis, a ship, perhaps recalling Saint Peter's ship or Noah's Ark. The norm for all later developments, early Christian, Byzantine, Norman, medieval, Renaissance, lies in the Roman basilica, with its wide central area and aisles and galleries divided by columns and arches. In the third and fourth centuries the apse was pushed back behind a transverse nave or transept, and later nave, transept and apse met under a dome or tower at the crossing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neve:
Neve was a titular see of Arabia, suffragan of Bostra. Two of its bishops are known: Petronius, who attended Ephesus in 431, and Jobius, present at Chalcedon in 451. Isaac, a third bishop named by Le Quien about 540, was not Neve's bishop but Nineve's, living at the end of the seventh century.

The Diocese of Neve appears in Antioch's sixth-century Notitia, and George of Cyprus mentions the city in the next century. The Revue biblique published Greek inscriptions from the locality. A large Muslim village called Nawa, in the Hauran, now occupies the former see's site, and the ancient Christian church's tower still stands visible. Neve must not be confused with Mount Nebo, about 94 miles south of the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-octave:
An octave, in liturgy, stretches a feast across eight days, though seven, not eight, rules Jewish festal reckoning. Each seventh day is a Sabbath, and the seventh month and year are sacred, and feasts like Azymes and Tabernacles last seven days, with Pentecost seven weeks after Passover.

Yet the eighth day kept its own role: circumcision fell on it, Tabernacles gained an eighth-day solemnity, and Temple dedications closed on it. The church took up that pattern, and the entry follows octaves from Jewish roots through Roman practice to their modern ranks and rules.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parasceve:
Parasceve, from the Greek for preparation, displaced the older prosabbaton and became the Hellenistic Jews' name for Friday. Greek church writers took it up after the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. Jews first applied it to Friday afternoon, then to the whole day, since preparations for the Sabbath had to be made, as the King James Bible's Day of Preparation shows.

Law's minute observance demanded three meals of choicest food ready before sunset, and barred Friday afternoon business that might spill into the Sabbath. Augustus freed Jews from certain legal duties from the ninth hour. Parasceve also marked eves of sabbatic feasts, above all Nisan 15, first day of unleavened bread, whose eve in Judea stopped work at noon and in Galilee freed the whole day. Later pages trace its liturgical uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-chome:
Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve was the founder of Montreal, born in Champagne early in the seventeenth century and dead at Paris on 9 September 1676. He served in the Dutch war at thirteen. Reading Jesuit Relations drew him to Canada. Jerome Lalemant proposed him to lead Royer de la Dauversiere's company to found Ville-Marie on Montreal island. Lauzon, the ex-governor, had ceded it for ten pounds of fish a year. Jeanne Mance, future foundress of the Hotel-Dieu, joined the party.

Governor Montmagny tried to stop the venture, holding the colonists at Sillery through winter 1641 to 1642. Maisonneuve landed on the island with his followers on 17 May 1642. Vimont said the first Mass, and the Blessed Sacrament stayed exposed all day, lit by fireflies in a phial. The colony, dedicated to the Virgin as Ville-Marie, stood at a waterways' crossing, ever alert against Iroquois attack.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-van-hov:
Peter van Hove was a Flemish Franciscan exegete, born at Rethy in the Campine and dying at Antwerp in 1793. Pupil of William Smits, founder of Antwerp's Musaeum Philologico-Sacrum, he trained Franciscan students in biblical languages, history, geography, and chronology for a critical, literal reading of Scripture. On Smits's death in 1770 he took over the flourishing school, which the French Revolution soon destroyed.

Before that post he published historical and archaeological theses. A 1765 portrait of first-century church life drew largely from Paul. Later works covered sacred images, the theocratic kingdom of Israel, and Christ as our Passover, the last giving an excellent Gospel chronology. His heavier labour was finishing Smits's Flemish Vulgate translation and commentary, sixteen folio volumes already edited when the task fell to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-genevieve:
Genevieve, patroness of Paris, saved her city twice: once by prayer against Attila, once by charity under siege. Born at Nanterre about 419 or 422 to Severus and Gerontia, likely respectable townspeople rather than poor peasants, she caught Germain of Auxerre's eye as a thoughtful child in 429. He foretold a life of sanctity drawing many virgins to God. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Paris to 512.

When Attila swept Gaul in 451, Parisians prepared to flee, but Genevieve urged penance and trust, promising the town would be spared. Attila turned toward Orléans, leaving Paris untouched. Years later, under Merowig's siege, her charity won clemency from Merowig, Childeric, and Clovis. She planned the church of Peter and Paul, begun by Clovis, where she was buried and miracles multiplied at her tomb.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-or-way-:
The state or way of the soul, purgative, illuminative, and unitive, maps Christian growth in grace. Theologians use state for a calling in life, as when Paul bids each man abide in the calling wherein he was called. States of perfection divide into clerical, religious, and secular, and religious states into contemplative, active, and mixed orders.

In a second sense state means stages of advancement in the supernatural life: the practice of all virtues, theological and moral, in outward and inward acts. Two elements combine: human effort and God's assisting grace, never wanting for acts God commands or inspires. Perfection advances with the energy and fidelity of souls answering grace. The purgative way cleanses sin, the illuminative enlightens the mind, and the unitive joins the soul to God in love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-carve:
Thomas Carve, whose true name was Carew, was an Irish historian born in County Tipperary in 1590 and probably dead by 1672. Ordained priest, he left Ireland as chaplain to an Irish regiment serving in Austria under Walter Butler, and later under Devereux. He marched through several campaigns of the Thirty Years' War, watching at first hand the events he would record.

His chief work, the Itinerarium, published at Mainz, Speyer and later London, gives a soldier-chaplain's account of that war. In 1640 he became chaplain to the English, Scottish and Irish forces in Austria, and from 1643 he lived at Vienna as a choral vicar of St. Stephen's Cathedral. His last book appeared at Sulzbach in 1672.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-occlev:
Thomas Occleve, also called Hoccleve, was an English poet born about 1368 who died in 1450. Almost all we know of him comes from his own poems. At about nineteen he took a clerkship in the Privy Seal Office, a post he held for at least twenty-four years. He drew a pension of ten pounds a year from 1399 and twenty pounds from 1424.

His La Male Regle of 1406 confesses a life of pleasure and dissipation, while his marriage in 1411 and his De Regimine Principum soon after show a reformed man. Linked always with Lydgate as a follower of Chaucer, he left three passages about Chaucer. He also left a portrait of him in the De Regimine manuscript, painted, he says, to keep the master's face in memory.
celsus-de-medicina-grieve:
James Grieve translated Celsus's De Medicina into English in 1756. Aulus Cornelius Celsus compiled the great Roman medical encyclopedia around 25 CE. Surgery, drugs, and diet all stand within his clear Latin survey.

Celsus gives the famous four signs of inflammation still taught today. Redness, swelling, heat, and pain define the condition in his words. He describes cataract surgery, bladder stones, and wound care in detail. Grieve's translation made the most readable ancient medical text English. Celsus was likely a gentleman compiler rather than a practicing doctor. His clarity preserved Greek medicine for Rome and for every century since.
christmas-eve:
Robert Browning's Christmas Eve is a long poem that begins on a stormy night outside a little country chapel. The speaker, kept waiting in the rain, squeezes into a crowded dissenting service and watches a congregation very different from himself.

From that chapel the poem moves outward, setting one way of worship against others and testing where true faith is found. Browning lets the speaker argue, doubt and imagine, so that the poem becomes a dramatic debate about belief rather than a simple nativity piece. Readers who know Browning's monologues will recognise the restless, questioning voice, and newcomers will find a vivid entry into Victorian religious argument.
crockett-narrative:
Davy Crockett published his Narrative of his own life in 1834, while serving in Congress from Tennessee. Crockett was already a folk hero of the frontier, and tall tales clung to his name. He wrote, he said, to tell the true story himself.

He recounts bear hunts, militia service under Andrew Jackson, and rough backwoods politics in his own spelling and slang. Humor runs through it all, even his feuds with President Jackson. Two years later Crockett died at the Alamo. The Narrative fixed his image as the coonskin-capped frontiersman, half real man and half legend of his own making.
cynthia-s-revels-or-the-fountain-of-self:
Ben Jonson wrote Cynthia's Revels as a court comedy in which Queen Cynthia judges courtiers drunk on self-love. Jonson, the sharpest wit of Shakespeare's London stage, aimed the satire at the Elizabethan court itself. Cynthia, a goddess figure standing for the queen, holds a revel that turns into a trial. A fountain has infected the courtiers with vanity.

Crites, a scholar with the author's own voice, watches fools parade their ruling follies. Amorphus, a traveler shapeless from copying every foreign fashion, tutors Asotus in nonsense. Anaides and other gallants boast, dance, and sing while their emptiness shows through the polish. Cynthia at last unmasks the company, fines the worst offenders, and orders a cleaner court. Songs and masque-like dances sweeten the attack for its audience. Readers find Jonson mixing flattery and rebuke in one glass: praise for the queen, scorn for the parasites around her throne.
december-love:
Robert Hichens's December Love is a novel of London society. It opens with Alick Craven, a Foreign Office man who has lived in the capital for years, apart from a spell of military service. Craven keeps interesting friends but holds himself apart from social bustle, a laziness that puzzles his acquaintance Francis Braybrooke.

Braybrooke knows everybody and delights in people above ideas. He takes pleasure in drawing new faces into his circle, and his talk sets the novel's social machinery in motion. Hichens watches how talk, introductions and reputations steer lives in drawing rooms and clubs, with Craven's reserve as the still centre. Readers who enjoy novels of manners, where character is revealed in conversation rather than action, will find December Love finely observed.

equiano-interesting-narrative:
Olaudah Equiano published his Interesting Narrative in 1789, and it became the founding text of the slave narrative. Equiano said he was born in West Africa, kidnapped as a boy, and carried across the Atlantic. The book sold widely and went through many editions in his lifetime.

He recounts the Middle Passage, years at sea with the Royal Navy, and his work as a sailor and trader. In 1766 he bought his freedom and later settled in London. There he joined the fight against the slave trade. His vivid, careful testimony helped shift British opinion toward abolition.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe: An FBI memorandum dated December 15, 1966 concerns the unauthorized electronic surveillance of Martin Luther King Jr. The Bureau's bugging of King became one of the great scandals of its domestic intelligence work. A headquarters memo calling such surveillance unauthorized, written while King still lived, is a rare paper from inside that campaign. The record gives the date and subject but no contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SalsbergDave_Sa:
A flyer announces a talk by Harold Weisberg on September 19, 1967. His subject is his book 'Photographic Whitewash,' his study of the photographic evidence in the Kennedy case. The host is the Men's Club of the Suburban Jewish Community Center in Havertown, Pennsylvania. The flyer gives the speaker, the book, the place, and the date.

Weisberg lived by such talks. Synagogue halls, college rooms, and community centers were his distribution network years before any internet. A printed flyer was how a room got filled. This one preserves the machinery of a speaking date in a Philadelphia suburb, less than four years after Dallas. It shows the assassination debate traveling at the speed of a mimeographed sheet.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneOliverJame: Harold Weisberg kept careful notes on July 22, 1992, after a phone call with lawyer Bill Pepper. Pepper, who represented James Earl Ray, wanted to involve film director Oliver Stone in The Trial of James Earl Ray project. Weisberg's memo records what was said and what was asked of him. It shows how the Ray case, the King assassination, and Hollywood's interest in both kept crossing paths decades later.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia: 'A Bloody, Expensive and Prolonged Coercive Effort': the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture on the US coercive campaign in Colombia. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
Jonathan Pollard, a former United States naval intelligence analyst, was convicted of spying for Israel and served thirty years in prison. This briefing book, posted in November 2020, revisits his case through declassified records. The posting calls it a still sensitive case, and the timing explains why.

Evidence here is limited to the date and subject, so detail must stay modest. What the record establishes is the Archive returning to a case that strained American-Israeli relations for decades. Pollard's parole and later move to Israel kept the file in the news, and declassified paper remains the firmest ground in a debate full of advocacy.
john-jago-s-ghost-or-the-dead-alive:
John Jago's Ghost, or The Dead Alive, is a mystery tale by Wilkie Collins, dated 1873. Its narrator, Philip Lefrank, is a young London barrister in good practice. The story opens in his chambers after he faints at his desk from overwork. His doctor finds no disease of heart or lungs, only a brain worn out by labor.

Rest, the doctor orders, or work will mean death within time. Lefrank resists, then breaks down in court, unable to gather facts and dates. He gives back his briefs and books passage on the first steamer for New York. A farming relative in America has long invited him. Collins sends his sick narrator across the Atlantic, where the mystery of John Jago waits.
ladies-must-live:
Alice Duer Miller published her novel Ladies Must Live with the Century Company in 1917. Paul Meylan drew its pictures. Miller had already won readers with Come Out of the Kitchen.

The title states the problem facing her heroines. Women with little money must still keep a place in society. The story mixes romance with sharp social comedy. Its scenes turn on manners, calls, and careful matches. Readers of light fiction from that era will find a witty, pointed tale about money and marriage. Illustrations mark key social scenes through the novel. Miller's dialogue carries much of the satire in quick, polished exchanges.
lady-hester-or-ursula-s-narrative:
Charlotte M. Yonge published Lady Hester, or Ursula's Narrative, in 1874. Ursula tells the story at her brothers' and sisters' request. She wants later generations to understand their strange family history.

Chapters move from Sault St. Pierre to Trevorsham and a peerage case. A white doe's warning, hunting scenes, and Trevor's legacy follow. Family claims, property, and honor drive the plot. Yonge frames the tale as a sober family record. That frame gives its surprises the feel of reported fact. Yonge sets private family honor against public legal claims. The peerage question gives old griefs a fresh, sharp edge.
last-poems-translations-from-the-book-of:
Laurence Hope published Last Poems as translations from the Book of Indian Love. Her real name was Adela Florence Cory, later Nicolson. A dedication to Malcolm Nicolson opens the book in verse.

She tells him her lighter love songs never spoke of him. Words inspired by him felt too sacred for strangers' lips. She praises his noble soul and generous law toward others. Sorrow, she says, had marked him before they met. The poems that follow carry love, loss, and an Indian setting. The dedication's grief gives the love poems a grave frame. Hope's lush images draw on Indian heat, flowers, and night.
laugh-and-live:
Douglas Fairbanks published Laugh and Live in New York in 1917. The film star dedicated it to his mother. Fourteen chapters turn his energy into advice on living well.

Early chapters urge an early start and learning from experience. Later ones praise honesty, cleanliness, and good reading. Fairbanks links success with laughter, energy, and a built-up personality. Self-indulgence, he warns, leads to failure. The book captures the cheerful self-help style of a silent film idol at his peak. Fairbanks's screen persona and his advice match closely here. Both promise that energy and good humor can be practiced daily.
life-in-the-grey-nunnery-at-montreal-an-:
Sarah J. Richardson presents herself here as an escaped nun. Her narrative claims to expose horrors, mysteries, and cruelties of convent life. Edward P. Hood edited the Montreal account for publication. Chapter heads promise a white nunnery, a nursery, and an orphan's home.

Later chapters allege starvation, a torture room, and punishment choices. Richardson recounts two escapes, a recapture, and a lonely midnight walk. Appendices attack Romanist practice in openly polemical terms. Readers should treat the book as her claimed testimony, written to persuade. A chapter called Alone with the Dead heightens her claimed ordeal. The sick nun and a superior's death add to the convent's horrors.
logic-deductive-and-inductive:
Carveth Read first published this logic textbook in June 1898. Grant Richards issued the first two editions in London. A fourth edition, enlarged and partly rewritten, followed later. Read also wrote The Metaphysics of Nature and moral studies.

His title promises both deductive and inductive logic together. The therefore symbol gets a special printer's representation here. Students of reasoning formed the book's intended audience. Repeated reprints through 1920 show its classroom durability. Simpkin, Marshall issued the enlarged fourth edition from Stationers' Hall Court. Reprints ran almost yearly through the book's first decades.
manalive:
Manalive is a novel by G. K. Chesterton, published by Thomas Nelson in 1912. Part One presents the enigmas of Innocent Smith. A great wind blows him, like a leaf, into Beacon House. His luggage, his banner, and his garden puzzle the other guests.

Part Two offers the explanations of Innocent Smith, charge by charge. He stands accused of murder, burglary, desertion, and polygamy. Each wild charge hides a joyful and innocent truth. Smith seems mad only because he loves life so fiercely. Chesterton turns farce into a hymn to ordinary existence. The book is his most exhilarating defense of wonder.
marie-a-story-of-russian-love:
Marie, a story of Russian love, is Alexander Pushkin's tale in Marie Zielinska's translation. Its hero is a young sergeant of the guards sent to a far fortress. His guide leads him through a snowstorm to stranger company. A duel, then love, fill his first months of service.

The captain's daughter, Marie, wins the young officer's heart. Then Pougatcheff's rebellion rises, and the fortress is assaulted. The rebel camp, a siege, and an arrest follow in swift chapters. Pushkin mixes a love story with Russia's great peasant rising. His prose is clear, swift, and quietly ironic. The tale is his finest work of historical fiction.
memories-a-story-of-german-love:
Max Muller's Memories: A Story of German Love appears here in George P. Upton's English. A. C. McClurg of Chicago printed it in 1902. Eight memories, from first to last, make up the short book.

Upton warns that translation must dim the beauty of any work. The German tale's charm lies in its elegant simplicity, he says. It has no plot, incidents, or staged scenes, he grants. Yet it holds interest, grace, and pathos from start to end, he argues. Plain German turned to plain English was the translator's aim. German idioms may linger, he grants, where grace would suffer more.
molly-make-believe:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott published this romantic comedy with the Century Company in 1911. Walter Tittle supplied the illustrations. Abbott dedicates the book to her silent partner. The illustration list hints at the story's world of Cornelia and messenger boys. One caption notes that every girl like Cornelia had to go South sometime.

Molly, the heroine, earns her name from make-believe. She writes bright, personal letters for a correspondence service, pretending friendship with lonely subscribers. One subscriber, housebound and skeptical, answers differently than the rest. Abbott turns the deception into a light, warm courtship, told largely through the letters themselves.
nasa-tm-19690014254-magnetometers-for-sp:
B. G. Ledley of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this May 1969 preprint, numbered X-611-69-156, on magnetometers for space use. It was prepared for a Paris conference that month on weak magnetic fields in geophysics and space. Spacecraft cross regions of wildly different field strength, from near planets to deep interplanetary space. Their magnetic sensors must stay accurate across that whole range.

Ledley describes the wide-range instruments Goddard built for that problem. The fifth Orbiting Geophysical Observatory carried two of them together. One was a rubidium vapor magnetometer, using optically pumped atoms. The other was a three-axis fluxgate with digital field compensation. Development work on both types at Goddard is also described.
nasa-tm-19700023046-performance-evaluati:
John B. Hall Jr. of the Langley Research Center in Virginia ran this evaluation of a water-recovery subsystem. The unit uses evaporation to win drinking water back from liquid wastes. It was designed for long crewed missions, where resupply is not possible.

Hall ran four long wick-life tests across a range of working conditions. In all, the unit processed hundreds of pounds of urine and flush water. He checked how urine collection and pretreatment changed the water quality. He also measured how solid buildup in the wicks wore the system down. The tests included the use of an automatic feed control.
nasa-tm-19700024451-some-performance-cha:
Harold R. Kaufman and Richard P. Vahrenkamp wrote this paper for a 1970 electric propulsion conference at Stanford. It reports performance traits of divergent-field bombardment thrusters. These are ion engines that use electron bombardment to make thrust.

The team ran a hands-on study of thrusters with strongly spread-out magnetic fields. Mercury served as the propellant in this line of work. Some traits of these engines had not been examined closely in years, they note. Ion engines push weakly but sip fuel, so they suit long missions. Knowing their true performance guides the design of the next engines.
nasa-tm-19710000763-paired-comparison-te:
J. Reece Roth and Walter M. Krawczonek of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a November 1970 plasma physics meeting in Washington. It compares two kinds of probes used to sense a turbulent plasma. The probes are the capacitive type and the floating Langmuir type.

The team made paired measurements of the wobble in the plasma's electric potential. The plasma sat steady inside a magnetic mirror device while they worked. Each probe type read the same plasma across a wide band of frequencies. Comparing the two side by side shows whether the cheaper or simpler probe can be trusted. Plasma labs depend on such checks for honest readings.
nasa-tm-19710002214-survey-of-materials-:
Arthur L. Smith of the Lewis Research Center wrote this survey in November 1970. It gathers what was known about materials for thermionic converters meant for space. A thermionic converter turns heat straight into electric power, with no moving parts.

Smith wrote the survey for readers new to the field, he states. He stresses how the choice of material shapes the behavior of the electrodes. The survey first sets out what the materials must do. It then names the materials most likely to meet those needs. Such converters were leading hopes for power far from the Sun.
nasa-tm-19720004516-mobility-systems-act:
Clyde S Jones Jr and Frank J Nola of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 9, 1971, as NASA TM X-64623. Both worked in the Astrionics Laboratory. It describes the mobility system of the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle. That system covers the wheels, motors, and drives that let astronauts roam the Moon. Marshall managed much of the rover's development work.

Special weight falls on the backup features of the design. The choice of drive motors also gets close attention. A summary chart reports how the rover performed on the Moon during Apollo 15. An appendix details Marshall work on high efficiency drive systems. It compares those systems with the one finally selected for flight.
nasa-tm-19720005575-silicon-controlled-r:
Arthur G Birchenough designed and built this power inverter, reported in December 1971 as NASA TM X-2442. The unit is a square wave inverter using silicon controlled rectifiers, or SCRs. It turns battery style direct current into alternating current for spacecraft loads. A commutation failure can leave an SCR stuck on and wreck the output. The design answers that risk directly.

A special circuit shuts the inverter down if commutation fails. Its power stage pairs two impulse commutated branches in parallel. The whole stage uses just six parts, a notably spare design. A four hundred watt breadboard version was built and tested. Simple, protected inverters mattered for space power systems of the period.
new-word-analysis-or-school-etymology-of:
William Swinton wrote New Word-Analysis as a school book on the roots of English words. The American Book Company copyrighted it in 1879, for use in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago schools. Swinton had won a gold medal for text books at the Paris Exposition of 1878. Practical exercises fill the book.

His preface calls it a new modeling of his Word-Analysis, first published in 1871. Teachers praised the old methods but wanted more practice work for pupils. Swinton kept the Latin roots and their lessons as a model of study. He then added more than two hundred Latin root words, with their chief English offshoots, plus drills in spelling and defining.
oscar-the-detective-or-dudie-dunne-the-e:
Oscar the Detective, issued in Old Sleuth's Special Detective Series for twenty-five cents in 1895, is a dime novel of New York low life. Its hero, Dudie Dunne, is billed as the exquisite detective. The first chapter shows his method: seeming to be exactly what he is not.

A dude of the first water strolls through a rough New York street, peering through his single eyeglass at the tenements. The little toughs on the corner see a strayed dandy and plan first fun, then plunder. Chapter one promises that when Simple John's mask comes off, the fur flies. The book is pure period pulp: disguise, slang, and street justice in weekly-novel form.
out-of-the-primitive:
Robert Ames Bennet's adventure novel Out of the Primitive, published in 1911 as a sequel to Into the Primitive, opens off the southeast coast of Africa. A little tramp rescue steamer lies to in the darkness north of the Zambezi. Coral reefs make moonless nights dangerous there. The Southern Cross scintillates over phosphorescent water. The offshore breeze carries the stench of the Mozambique swamps.

The Right Honorable the Earl of Avondale — Lord James — comes on deck before dawn in snowy linen, as crisp as the officer Meggs is bluff. The frontispiece shows what awaits: Lord James dropped without a groan, and a woman gasping, you coward, you murderer. Bennet wrote castaway melodrama for the age of empire, and the castaways of chapter one sail straight into it.
podcast-joerogan-DE9oFxGoMvE:
Podcaster Darryl Cooper joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2289. Cooper makes long history series that retell famous events from a revisionist angle, and he has drawn both praise and fire for it. Rogan gives him the long format to explain his approach.

Cooper talks about how he reads the standard stories of war and power, and where he thinks they mislead. Rogan asks about the backlash his work draws and the line between fresh eyes and distortion. The episode lets listeners judge a controversial historian in his own words, rather than through the clips his critics share.
red-eve:
H. Rider Haggard first published this romance in 1911 and dedicated it to Dr. Jehu, his fellow commissioner on coast defense. The two had spent five years seeking ways to guard coasts from the sea and to make swamps fertile. Haggard wrote the tale in the gaps of that work, and says so in his dedication letter of May 27, 1911.

The story opens in the days before Crécy, when Edward the Third sat on England's throne. Doom comes from the East, from far Cathay, and no word of it has reached the West. In a snowbound city, fires burn the bodies of thousands, for pestilence is king there. Red Eve, the dauntless heroine, and Murgh, Gateway of the Gods, stand at the tale's heart.
remarks-of-mr-calhoun-of-south-carolina-:
John C. Calhoun of South Carolina spoke in the United States Senate on February 15, 1833, on nullification and the Force Bill. He begins with the public debt, all but paid, and the hope of relief that died with it. The tariff settlement that followed, he charges, cut duties in a way that laid the burden more unevenly than the Act of 1828.

Duties so arranged, he argues, act as bounties on one side and taxes on the other. The two great sections of the country were thus set in direct conflict. South Carolina, denied relief, chose to use her reserved powers, called a convention, and adopted her ordinance.
saint-bartholomew-s-eve: G. A. Henty wrote Saint Bartholomew's Eve, a tale of the Huguenot Wars headed with the year 1894, with pictures by H. J. Draper. The contents list a preface and chapters opening with Driven from Home, An Important Decision, and In a French Chateau. Later chapters include An Experiment, Taking the Field, The Battle of Saint Denis, and A Rescue. The list shown here runs on to The Third Huguenot War and An Important Mission as the ninth chapter.
sweetapple-cove:
George Van Schaigk wrote Sweetapple Cove, dated 1914. The novel is told from the diary of John Grant. Grant is a young doctor. He has shaken the dust of the great city by the Hudson off his feet. He leaves rich laboratories, vast hospitals, and rising prospects behind on a sudden whim.

Grant now lives in a little house at Sweetapple Cove. The people speak with an accent the outside world has forgotten. A kind housewife lets him the two best rooms. The rent is so small that he is ashamed to offer it. He is the cove's only boarder and only doctor. Word of him spreads from fishing smack to fishing smack along the bleak coast, and patients begin coming in droves to his door.
taken-alive:
Volume Eleven of the works of E. P. Roe holds Taken Alive and Other Stories, with an autobiography, in an illustrated printing. An opening piece, A Native Author Called Roe, introduces the writer before the title tale begins in five chapters.

Taken Alive moves from Something Before Unknown through A Visitor at the Mine and Thwarted to What Brandt Saw Christmas Eve. A second long story, Found Yet Lost, follows love in the wilderness and love at home through disability, second bloom, and a Civil War chapter called Forward! Company A. Shorter pieces include Queen of Spades, A Christmas-Eve Suit, Three Thanksgiving Kisses, Susie Rolliffe's Christmas, and Jeff's Treasure. Roe's tales mix mines, soldiers, and home life with a minister's moral warmth.
the-adventure-of-the-dying-detective:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of the Dying Detective as a Sherlock Holmes tale, told by Dr. Watson. Rather than open with a client, Watson opens with Mrs. Hudson, the long-suffering landlady of Baker Street.

Her first-floor flat, he says, is raided at all hours by odd and shady guests, while Holmes fills it with mess, odd-hour music, indoor revolver practice, and foul science trials. Yet his pay is princely, and she holds him in awe mixed with fond regard for his courtesy to women. Readers then get a tale where Holmes lies near death from a rare disease, and Watson must fetch the one man who can help — who is also a foe.
the-american-prejudice-against-color-an-:
William G. Allen, who styles himself a refugee from American despotism, published this account in London in 1853 with W. and F. G. Cash, alongside sellers in Edinburgh and Dublin. Its subtitle promises to show how easily the nation got into an uproar over race.

A preface prints a letter dated March 23, 1853, from Congressman Gerrit Smith of New York to Joseph Sturge of Birmingham. Smith introduces Allen, his much esteemed friend and a professor, as a man of great mental and moral worth. He hopes the English visit will prove both useful and happy for him.
the-bravest-of-the-brave:
G. A. Henty opens The Bravest of the Brave, dated 1896, with a preface to his dear lads on a lost hero. Few great chiefs, he says, have sunk so deep out of mind as the Earl of Peterborough. His time as a general spanned just over a year. In that span he showed a gift for war that has never been topped.

Why so faint a mark on the past? Marlborough's fame and wins threw a shade on him, Henty says. His cause could scarcely be called England's, and the folk cared little for it. The war's aim was balked, through no fault of his. Worst of all, his gift had no fixed aim, and he quarreled with near each man he met. Yet he was warm, kind to those below him, and prized by his troops.
the-case-of-mrs-clive: The Case of Mrs. Clive, a work of Catherine Clive dated 1744, is presented here by the Augustan Reprint Society in an edition with an introduction by Richard C. Frushell. Notes trace its verse and emblem to George Wither's Collection of Emblems of 1635. Its quoted lines are traced to Dryden. The society's general editors are also named. They sit at the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library and the University of California, Los Angeles. No page of Clive's own text is shown.
the-czar-s-spy-the-mystery-of-a-silent-l: Chevalier William Le Queux, author of The Closed Book, subtitled The Czar's Spy the mystery of a silent love, in an edition dated 1905. Its contents list seventeen chapters with titles such as His Britannic Majesty's Service, Why the Safe Was Opened, The Castle of the Terror, The Strangler, and The Truth about the Lola. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-dead-alive: Wilkie Collins's The Dead Alive, dated 1873, is shown here only through its contents, which list twelve chapters. Among them are The Sick Man, The New Faces, The Moonlight Meeting, The Beechen Stick, and The News from Narrabee. The rest are The Lime-Kiln, The Materials in the Defense, The Confession, The Advertisement, The Sheriff and the Governor, The Pebble and the Window, and The End of It. Only the title page, contents, and the heading of Chapter I are present here; a companion record opens with the chapter itself.
the-dream-detective:
Sax Rohmer's The Dream Detective, dated 1920, gives some account of the methods of Moris Klaw. Its contents list nine cases in episode form. They run from the tragedies in the Greek room and the potsherd of Anubis to the Crusader's ax, an ivory statue, and the Blue Rajah.

Later cases name whispering poplars, a chord in G, headless mummies, and the haunting of Grange. Klaw is a dream sleuth who lies down at crime scenes and reads the past in sleep. Rohmer blends crime, the occult, and rich antiques. Klaw never hurries, and his calm chills suspects.
the-egoist-a-comedy-in-narrative:
George Meredith's The Egoist, subtitled A Comedy in Narrative, opens with a prelude on the Comic Spirit. Comedy, Meredith says, plays its game in drawing rooms, hunting the spirit in men and women without dust or crash. Behind all stands the Book of Egoism, the world's biggest book, which each age keeps writing and which comedy must squeeze into shape.

Sir Willoughby Patterne, rich and self-pleased, courts Clara Middleton while his past vows entangle him. Meredith's dense, bright prose turns courtship into a duel of wits. The novel is his most famed study of male vanity.
the-empire-of-love:
W. J. Dawson's The Empire of Love, copyrighted in 1907 by Fleming H. Revell, is set for M. M. D., who, Dawson says, lived the book's teaching in two London years of kind toil for the lost. A line from Thomas à Kempis heads the contents: love feels no burden and pleads no impossibility. The first chapter is named The Genius to Be Loved.

Dawson, a famed preacher, argues that love, not force or scorn, redeems lives sunk in vice. His chapters join pulpit warmth with street-level tales of rescue. The book aims at workers among the poor.
the-evolution-of-love:
Emil Lucka's The Evolution of Love, in Ellie Schleussner's English rendering first issued in Great Britain in 1922, traces love through three stages. The first is the sexual instinct. The second, love proper, opens with the birth of Europe, then the deification of woman in the troubadours, the Queen of Heaven, Dante and Goethe, and Michel Angelo.

A third part turns to perversions of that high strain: brides of Christ and sexual mystics. Lucka, an Austrian thinker, reads poems, cults, and lives as signs of one slow growth. His scheme is bold, dated, and rich in learning.
the-fatal-glove:
Clara Augusta wrote The Fatal Glove, printed in 1892, a tale that starts with a poor boy in New York. A short second tale, Constitutionally Bashful, follows it, with no author named.

Arch Trevlyn, a small street sweeper, ends a wet day with a pocket of pennies and a glad heart. He saves for tea, milk, sugar, and an orange for his frail mother, then longs for one white rose like those of her youth. A rude clerk drives him from the flower shop as a thief. Pride, poverty, and a son's love set the tale in motion.
the-fugitive:
Rabindranath Tagore wrote The Fugitive as a set of poems and short verse plays, giving the book to W. W. Pearson. Three parts divide the work, each mixing a tale with translations.

The tales named are Kacha and Devayani, Ama and Vinayaka, Somaka and Ritvik, and Karna and Kunti, drawn from old Indian story. The first poem hails an eternal fugitive whose rush frets space into bubbles of light, and asks if his heart is lost to a lover who calls across vast loneliness. Tagore turns myth and longing into song that seeks God in flight and in return.
the-glory-of-the-conquered-the-story-of-: Susan Glaspell wrote The Glory of the Conquered. Its subtitle is The Story of a Great Love. The book is dated 1909. Glaspell dedicated it to Dr. A. L. Hageboeck. She said he made the book possible. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in two parts. The heads name Ernestine and Karl in his laboratory. They name Ernestine in her studio. They treat science, art, and love. The second part names marriage, a blind man's twilight, and love challenging fate.
the-guns-of-bull-run-a-story-of-the-civi: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Guns of Bull Run, a story of the Civil War's eve. It belongs to his Civil War Series. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of the series, and a list of principal characters. The characters center on two cousins. Harry Kenton is a lad who fights on the Southern side. Dick Mason, his cousin, fights on the Northern side. Commanders and friends fill out the list.
the-history-of-david-grieve:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote The History of David Grieve, and she is named on the title page as the author of Robert Elsmere. The book is dedicated to the dear memory of her mother. Contents divide the life into four books: Childhood, Youth, Storm and Stress, and Maturity. Book one, chapter one opens on stone steps outside a small grey house.

A tall, bony woman holds out a battered hat and scolds Louie for always leaving something behind. Louie tells David to fetch it, and the boy goes back and takes the hat without protest. The woman warns that Louie would lose her head if it were loose, then returns inside. Dialect speech, a leafless garden, and a strict household set the childhood world.
the-kingdom-of-love: Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathered her poems in this volume. The copy comes from the 1909 Gay and Hancock edition of London. Only the title page and contents are present here. The poems themselves do not appear. The contents list the title poem first. Meg's Curse, Solitude, The Gossips, and Platonic follow. Grandpa's Christmas comes early too. Later pieces include After the Engagement and The Suicide. A Servian legend, The Falling of Thrones, and Her Last Letter appear. A Baby in the House and The Two Glasses close the list shown.
the-luck-of-roaring-camp-and-other-tales: Bret Harte's The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Tales appears here in the Riverside Edition. A publishers' note dated Boston, autumn 1902, explains that it rests on the fourteen-volume collection of 1897, enlarged with later work. Only that note and the contents are present here, so the tales themselves do not appear. The contents list the title sketch with The Outcasts of Poker Flat, Miggles, Tennessee's Partner, and Brown of Calaveras. Then comes a section of Condensed Novels, Harte's parodies, and earlier sketches including M'liss, an idyl of Red Mountain.
the-peace-negotiations-a-personal-narrat: Robert Lansing wrote The Peace Negotiations, a personal narrative of the Paris peace conference after the First World War. Front matter and a contents list are present, and no chapter text follows. The list opens with his reasons for writing. Chapters treat President Wilson's presence at the conference and the rival plans for a League of Nations. Self-determination, the system of mandates, and secret diplomacy follow. The Shantung settlement and the Bullitt affair close the list.
the-price-of-love: Arnold Bennett's tale The Price of Love, dated 1914, is shown through its contents page. The chapters themselves are not on view. Eighteen chapters are listed, and their titles sketch a plot of money and marriage. Money in the House opens the book, and Louis' Discovery and The Feast follow. In the Night, News of the Night, and Theories of the Theft point to a crime at the centre. Later titles include The Cinema, The Married Woman, and Runaway Horses. Dead-Lock, The Letter, and In the Monastery close the list.
the-return-of-the-native: Hardy's 1878 Return of the Native traps Eustacia on bleak Egdon Heath. Fate closes. The Tower library holds the full text. It heaved with heath. Lovers schemed. Heath endured. Doom fell. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-velvet-glove: Henry Seton Merriman, whose real name was Hugh Stowell Scott, wrote The Velvet Glove as a thirty-chapter novel. This record presents the contents and a list of illustrations, so the story's text does not appear. Early chapters move through a city of winds, high walls, a pilgrimage, and a figure called the Jade. Middle headings promise a royal adventure, a cloister, and Our Lady of the Shadows. Later titles include Cousin Peligros, Juanita Grows Up, and War's Alarm. French chapter titles close the list beside a casting vote.
the-woman-in-the-alcove:
Anna Katharine Green's The Woman in the Alcove opens with a list of twenty-three chapters. Their titles promise a diamond, gloves, an arrest, and a trap. The narrator begins by calling herself the plainest girl at a grand ball. Until one o'clock she was also the happiest person there. Then her world crumbled, and she sets out to explain why.

She has just earned a nurse's diploma after three years of training. Love, she insists, never figured in her plans. She doubts her looks could invite it. Green's mystery turns that quiet self-image upside down. Readers get a murder puzzle narrated by an unlikely witness at its center.
the-woman-in-white-with-original-illustr: A contents listing for an illustrated edition of Wilkie Collins's The Woman in White is all that appears here. The listing promises an introduction on Collins and his world. Prefaces from 1860 and 1861 are also named. The first epoch begins with Walter Hartright's story. Chapter numbers follow without the chapters themselves, so the novel cannot be read from these pages.

Mark Twain prefaced his detective story by insisting its strange incidents are facts taken from an old Swedish criminal trial, moved to America. truth-narrative:
Sojourner Truth, born enslaved in New York, could not read or write, so she dictated her Narrative, printed in 1850. Olive Gilbert, a white friend, took down her words. Truth sold the book at her talks to support herself.

She tells of her childhood in a Dutch-speaking household, the sale of her children, and her escape in 1826. A lawsuit won back her son Peter, a rare victory for an enslaved mother. She then took her new name and preached across the North. The Narrative stands behind her fame as an abolitionist and women's rights speaker.

youth-a-narrative:
Joseph Conrad wrote this sea tale, told by his narrator Marlow to friends around a table. All five men had begun life in the merchant service. That shared past binds them more than yachting ever could, Conrad writes. Marlow recalls his first voyage to the East as second mate. It was also his captain's first command. The voyage seemed made to picture life itself, he says.

Men fight, sweat, and nearly kill themselves to achieve something, Marlow reflects, and still fail through no fault. A cargo of coal becomes the test case. Readers get a young sailor's hard education in endurance, pride, and the indifference of the sea.
